prompt:
# Lesson Reconciliation Prompt

## Mission

Support the two internal Lesson Reconciliation tasks for exactly one Lesson:

- `lesson_candidate_clustering`: group candidate IDs only.
- `lesson_cluster_evaluation`: evaluate one validated cluster or a small batch
  of validated clusters into clean lesson-local teachable concepts.
- `lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`: repair a deterministic Phase 4b
  quality failure for targeted candidates only.

The input candidates come from Self-study Extraction and Metadata-only
Extraction. There is no top-down lesson extraction in this pipeline branch.

## Quick Start

First inspect `task`.

If `task` is `lesson_candidate_clustering`, return clusters only. Every
`input_candidate_ids` item must appear exactly once across cluster `candidate_ids`.
Do not create accepted concepts, pruning decisions, evidence, or provenance.

If `task` is `lesson_cluster_evaluation`, read the provided `clusters`,
`candidates`, and `input_candidate_ids`. Create the smallest clean set of
lesson-local concepts for those clusters only. Return accepted concepts plus one
`candidate_assignments` row for every input ID in the batch.

If `task` is `lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`, read the quality audit,
current reconciled candidates, and target candidates. Decide whether each target
candidate should be represented by a new accepted concept, merged into an
existing accepted concept, or pruned. Do not return `review`.

## Concept Standard

A lesson-local concept is one teachable idea small enough for the Companion to
check with one to three focused questions. It is not a source title, activity,
workbook label, technology name, vague topic, name-drop, incidental mention, or
tiny fragment that belongs inside a stronger concept.

Source-backed does not automatically mean lesson-worthy. A candidate can be
grounded in a source and still be incidental, off-lesson, too broad,
administrative, setup-oriented, or better represented inside another concept.
Accept only candidates that fit the Lesson's title, description, related labels,
and candidate evidence as teachable content for this Lesson.

## Clustering Workflow

1. Group duplicates and near-duplicates that likely describe the same teachable
   idea in this Lesson.
2. Keep distinct prerequisite, implementation, evaluation, or application ideas
   in separate clusters.
3. Prefer small coherent clusters over broad topic buckets.
4. Put operational setup, installation, licensing, career, administrative, and
   generic programming candidates in their own clusters unless the Lesson
   metadata clearly makes them central content.
5. Do not prune during clustering unless an input is clearly unrelated to the
   Lesson; if uncertain, put it in its own cluster for evaluation.
6. Every input candidate ID must appear exactly once across all clusters. Never
   emit empty clusters or invented candidate IDs.

## Evaluation Workflow

1. Treat Source Body candidates as the strongest evidence.
2. Merge duplicates and near-duplicates across Self-studies when they teach the
   same idea inside the provided cluster batch.
3. Split compound or messy candidates into cleaner accepted concepts when one
   input candidate supports multiple teachable ideas.
4. Accept Metadata-only candidates only when Workbook Metadata fills a real
   lesson gap not already covered by Source Body candidates.
5. Prefer lesson coherence over source-by-source preservation, but never drop a
   source-backed candidate silently.
6. Preserve useful granularity. Do not merge distinct definitions, pipeline
   steps, limitations, implementation methods, evaluation methods, or
   applications merely because they share a broad topic.
7. Reject off-lesson or low-transfer material even when it is source-backed:
   setup commands, environment configuration, licensing/legal administration,
   certification/career advice, repository mechanics, dataset download
   utilities, and routine file I/O should be accepted only when the Lesson
   metadata clearly makes that material central teachable content.
8. Use `used_in` when a candidate directly supports one or more accepted
   concepts.
9. Use `merged_into` when a candidate should not stand alone but is represented
   by one accepted concept.
10. Use `pruned` only when the candidate should not influence the lesson concept
   set at all. Use only a reason from `controlled_pruning_reasons`.
11. Do not prune a distinct teachable idea as a duplicate unless an accepted
   concept in this same response actually represents it. Never justify pruning
   by saying another cluster, later batch, or future step will handle the idea.
12. Avoid `review`. Phase 4 has no human review escape hatch. If the lesson
   metadata, candidate description, source roles, and coverage criteria are
   sufficient, decide accepted, merged, or pruned.
13. Use `review` only when the input is structurally impossible to interpret.
   Phase 4b will treat any review output as unresolved work requiring repair.

## Quality Repair Workflow

For `task: lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`:

1. Evaluate only `target_candidate_ids`; do not rewrite the whole Lesson.
2. Use `current_reconciled_candidates` to decide whether a target candidate is
   already represented.
3. Create `new_accepted_concepts` only for target candidates that represent
   lesson-worthy teachable ideas not already covered.
4. Use `existing_concept_candidate_additions` when a target candidate is
   represented by an existing reconciled concept.
5. Use `pruned` only when the target candidate should not influence the Lesson.
6. Never return `review`. A hard choice must still become accepted, merged, or
   pruned with a clear explanation.
7. Do not use a duplicate or near-duplicate reason unless the target candidate
   is represented by an existing or new accepted concept in this response.
8. If the audit flags `over_pruned`, re-check pruned target candidates for
   lesson-local definitions, methods, steps, limitations, evaluations, or
   applications that were lost by an overly broad pruning decision.
9. If the audit flags `over_merged`, split target candidates out of broad
   accepted concepts when they contain distinct lesson-local ideas.
10. If the audit flags `fragmented_duplicates`, merge duplicate accepted
   concepts by assigning target candidates to the best existing concept.
11. If the audit flags `metadata_overreach`, accept metadata-only targets only
   when they fill a lesson gap not already covered by source-body evidence.
12. If the audit flags `off_lesson_accepted`, prune setup, repository,
   administration, download, career, or generic tooling material unless the
   Lesson metadata clearly makes it central teachable content.
13. If the audit flags `over_accepted`, re-check whether target candidates
   should be merged into stronger accepted concepts or pruned for low teaching
   value.

## Clustering Output Contract

For `task: lesson_candidate_clustering`, return one valid JSON object only:

```json
{
  "clusters": [
    {
      "id": "cluster_001",
      "label": "Short cluster label",
      "rationale": "Why these candidates may describe the same teachable idea.",
      "candidate_ids": ["compact-candidate-id"]
    }
  ]
}
```

## Evaluation Output Contract

For `task: lesson_cluster_evaluation`, return one valid JSON object only. Cover
all candidates in the provided cluster batch:

```json
{
  "accepted_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "lr001",
      "label": "Specific lesson-local teachable idea",
      "description": "What the student needs to understand in this Lesson.",
      "coverage_criteria": ["Observable check in one to three focused questions."],
      "source_candidate_ids": ["compact-candidate-id"],
      "merge_rationale": "Why these candidates form one lesson-local concept."
    }
  ],
  "candidate_assignments": [
    {
      "candidate_id": "compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "used_in",
      "accepted_ids": ["lr001"]
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "represented-candidate-id",
      "status": "merged_into",
      "merged_into": "lr001",
      "explanation": "Why it is represented by lr001 instead of standing alone."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "discarded-candidate-id",
      "status": "pruned",
      "reason": "incidental",
      "explanation": "Why this candidate should not influence the lesson set."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "discarded-candidate-id",
      "status": "pruned",
      "reason": "unrelated",
      "explanation": "Why this candidate should not influence the lesson set."
    }
  ]
}
```

## Quality Repair Output Contract

For `task: lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`, return one valid JSON object
only:

```json
{
  "new_accepted_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "repair001",
      "label": "Specific lesson-local teachable idea",
      "description": "What the student needs to understand in this Lesson.",
      "coverage_criteria": ["Observable check in one to three focused questions."],
      "source_candidate_ids": ["target-compact-candidate-id"],
      "merge_rationale": "Why these target candidates form a lesson-local concept."
    }
  ],
  "existing_concept_candidate_additions": [
    {
      "reconciled_candidate_id": "existing-final-reconciled-candidate-id",
      "candidate_ids": ["target-compact-candidate-id"],
      "explanation": "Why the target candidate is already represented."
    }
  ],
  "candidate_assignments": [
    {
      "candidate_id": "target-compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "used_in",
      "accepted_ids": ["repair001"],
      "explanation": "Why this target candidate is accepted."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "target-compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "merged_into",
      "merged_into": "existing-final-reconciled-candidate-id",
      "explanation": "Why this target candidate is represented by an existing concept."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "target-compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "pruned",
      "reason": "low_teaching_value",
      "explanation": "Why this target candidate should not influence the lesson set."
    }
  ]
}
```

## Self-check

- For clustering, every `input_candidate_ids` item appears exactly once across
  all cluster `candidate_ids`.
- For evaluation, every `input_candidate_ids` item appears exactly once in
  `candidate_assignments`.
- Every `used_in` or `merged_into` assignment references accepted concept IDs
  that also list that candidate in `source_candidate_ids`.
- A candidate may support multiple accepted concepts with `used_in`.
- A `pruned` or `review` candidate must not appear in any accepted concept's
  `source_candidate_ids`.
- Every pruned near-duplicate must be represented by an accepted concept in this
  response, or it should not be pruned as a duplicate.
- For quality repair, every `target_candidate_ids` item appears exactly once in
  `candidate_assignments`, and no assignment has `status: review`.
- If several accepted concepts are mainly setup, environment, licensing,
  administration, career guidance, or generic programming basics, re-check the
  Lesson metadata before accepting them.
- Before returning, ask whether the accepted concept set would let the Companion
  tutor the Lesson described by the metadata without major off-topic detours or
  missing central teachable distinctions.
- Do not emit dependencies, lesson segments, final Concept IDs, bridge concepts,
  subject-level merge decisions, or runtime graph fields.

lesson.title: Introdução a Rede Neural
lesson.description: Este encontro tem por objetivo apresentar as Redes Neurais para as pessoas desenvolvedoras. A sua concepção, aplicação, algoritmos de treinamento e evolução serão abordadas. Com o término da instrução, espera-se que as pessoas desenvolvedoras possam estar mais familiarizadas com a forma como as Redes Neurais são desenvolvidas.

repair_plan.explanation: Review is not allowed as a final Phase 4 state.

target_candidates.label: Rede Neural Artificial
target_candidates.description: Uma rede neural artificial é um modelo preditivo baseado na dinâmica do cérebro, composto por neurônios conectados que realizam cálculos sobre entradas e produzem saídas.
coverage_criteria: O estudante deve ser capaz de definir o que é uma rede neural artificial e descrever seus componentes básicos (neurônios, conexões, função de ativação).

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: O capítulo começa definindo redes neurais artificiais como modelos preditivos inspirados no cérebro, com neurônios que disparam após cálculos ponderados.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Este conceito é amplo o suficiente para cobrir a definição fundamental, mas limitado para não incluir treinamento ou tipos específicos, permitindo verificação com poucas perguntas.

target_candidates.label: Neural Network Taxonomy (Chart Overview)
target_candidates.description: A summary chart presenting a wide variety of neural network architectures, including feedforward, recurrent, and generative models, as well as their components like memory cells and convolution kernels.
coverage_criteria: Name and briefly describe at least three distinct architectures shown in the chart.
Identify the arrow-based notation used to differentiate network types.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The chart itself is a visual taxonomy of neural networks, listing over 20 architectures and their interconnections.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This candidate focuses on the overall organization and overview provided by the chart, which is a single teachable concept.

anchors: A mostly complete chart of Neural Networks

current_reconciled_candidates.label: McCulloch-Pitts neuron model
current_reconciled_candidates.description: The first computational model of a neuron proposed by McCulloch and Pitts in 1943, representing neurons as simple electrical circuits with binary outputs.
coverage_criteria: Identify McCulloch and Pitts as the authors of the first formal neuron model in 1943.
Describe the basic idea of a simplified neuron with binary output.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Single candidate defines the concept.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Hebbian learning
current_reconciled_candidates.description: The principle that neural connections are strengthened when the pre- and post-synaptic neurons fire together, introduced by Donald Hebb in 1949 and later formalized as a learning rule.
coverage_criteria: State Hebb's postulate: 'neurons that fire together wire together'.
Give one example of a Hebbian-like learning rule.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Both candidates describe the same foundational learning principle; c45 provides the historical introduction and c46 elaborates on variations.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Perceptron
current_reconciled_candidates.description: A single-layer neural network model by Frank Rosenblatt (1958) that computes a weighted sum of inputs, subtracts a threshold, and outputs a binary class; it defines a linear decision boundary.
coverage_criteria: Explain the perceptron architecture: inputs, weights, bias, activation (step function).
State that the perceptron performs binary classification and can learn simple linearly separable patterns.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: All three candidates describe the perceptron, either historically (c45, c50) or architecturally (c46); together they cover its origins, mechanism, and fundamental role.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: ADALINE and MADALINE
current_reconciled_candidates.description: Early adaptive linear neural networks (ADALINE, MADALINE) developed by Widrow and Hoff (1959) that used adaptive linear elements; MADALINE was the first neural network applied to a real-world problem (echo cancellation).
coverage_criteria: Explain what ADALINE and MADALINE stand for.
Identify echo cancellation as the first real-world application of a neural network (MADALINE).
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Single candidate provides sufficient detail.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Minsky & Papert critique and the AI winter
current_reconciled_candidates.description: The 1969 book 'Perceptrons' by Minsky and Papert proved the limitations of single-layer perceptrons, leading to a halt in neural network funding and research throughout the 1970s.
coverage_criteria: Explain that Minsky and Papert demonstrated the inability of perceptrons to solve non-linearly separable problems (like XOR), causing a funding freeze.
Define the term 'AI winter' in the context of neural networks.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Single candidate captures the event.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Hopfield networks and the revival of neural network research
current_reconciled_candidates.description: John Hopfield's 1982 paper and the US-Japan Conference on Cooperative Competitive Neural Networks rekindled interest and funding in neural networks, ending the AI winter.
coverage_criteria: State that Hopfield's 1982 approach and the US-Japan conference helped restart neural network funding.
Mention that the conference and the Japanese fifth-generation project spurred renewed investment.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Single candidate defines the revival.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
current_reconciled_candidates.description: A specialized recurrent neural network architecture using gated memory cells (forget, input, output gates) to learn long-term dependencies and mitigate the vanishing gradient problem; introduced by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber in 1997.
coverage_criteria: Explain the purpose of an LSTM: to handle long-term dependencies in sequences.
Name the three gates and their basic roles (forget, input, output).
Contrast LSTM with a simple RNN in terms of memory capability.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: c45 introduces LSTM historically, c46 provides architectural details, and c47 explains the gate types; together they form a complete lesson-local concept.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Backpropagation
current_reconciled_candidates.description: The core learning algorithm for neural networks that computes the gradient of the loss function with respect to weights using the chain rule and updates weights in the opposite direction to minimize error.
coverage_criteria: List the four main steps of backpropagation: forward pass, loss computation, backward pass (gradient calculation), weight update.
Explain the role of the chain rule in propagating gradients from output to input layers.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: All candidates describe the backpropagation algorithm across different sources and languages; they reinforce the same teachable steps. The LeCun paper candidate (c45_pro_thinking_008) is pruned as an incidental application.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Feedforward neural network architecture
current_reconciled_candidates.description: A neural network organized into sequential layers (input, hidden, output) where connections flow only forward without cycles; each neuron computes a weighted sum plus bias followed by an activation function.
coverage_criteria: Sketch a diagram of a feedforward network with at least one hidden layer.
Explain the function of weights and biases in a feedforward neuron.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: All candidates describe the layered, feedforward structure; c49 is the Portuguese-language equivalent.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) basics
current_reconciled_candidates.description: A neural network architecture with feedback connections that pass information from one time step to the next, creating an internal memory suitable for sequential data.
coverage_criteria: Explain how recurrent loops distinguish RNNs from feedforward networks.
Give an example of a task that benefits from recurrent architecture (e.g., language modeling, time series prediction).
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Single candidate defines the concept.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Autoencoder
current_reconciled_candidates.description: An unsupervised neural network that compresses input into a lower-dimensional representation (encoding) and reconstructs the original input (decoding), useful for dimensionality reduction and feature learning.
coverage_criteria: Sketch the encoder-bottleneck-decoder structure.
Explain how an autoencoder can be used for data compression or denoising.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Single candidate provides the definition.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)
current_reconciled_candidates.description: A framework where a generator network creates synthetic data and a discriminator network tries to distinguish it from real data; adversarial training improves both.
coverage_criteria: Explain the roles of the generator and discriminator.
Describe the adversarial training process as a two-player game.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Single candidate defines the concept.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Activation Functions
current_reconciled_candidates.description: Non-linear activation functions (sigmoid, tanh, ReLU, step, softmax) applied to neuron outputs introduce non-linearity into the network, enabling learning of complex patterns. The sigmoid maps any real to (0,1); tanh to (-1,1); ReLU outputs max(0,x); step produces binary output.
coverage_criteria: List at least three activation functions with their formulas and typical output ranges.
Explain why non-linear activation functions are necessary in hidden layers.
Compare ReLU with sigmoid in terms of gradient flow and practical usage.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates describe various activation functions, their formulas, and their roles, together forming a single coherent teachable concept on activation functions.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Loss Functions
current_reconciled_candidates.description: Loss functions quantify the prediction error during training, guiding weight updates. Mean squared error is used for regression, binary cross-entropy for classification; logistic loss is commonly used for binary classification.
coverage_criteria: Match loss functions (MSE, binary cross-entropy) to the appropriate problem type.
Write the logistic loss formula and explain its intuition.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Both cover the purpose and specifics of loss functions, with one providing general types and the other focusing on logistic loss.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Convolutional Neural Networks
current_reconciled_candidates.description: CNNs are architectures for grid-structured data (e.g., images) that use convolutional layers to detect spatial features, pooling layers to reduce dimensionality, and fully-connected layers for classification. Output size depends on input, filter, stride, and padding.
coverage_criteria: Describe the operation of a convolutional layer (filter, stride, feature map).
Compute the output size of a convolutional layer given input dimensions, filter size, and padding.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: c47_pro_thinking_006 adds practical output size computation to the CNN overview, completing the teachable concept.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Deep Residual Networks
current_reconciled_candidates.description: Deep Residual Networks (DRNs) use skip connections (residual blocks) to allow gradients to flow through very deep architectures, mitigating the vanishing gradient problem and enabling training of networks like ResNet.
coverage_criteria: Explain what a residual block is and why it helps train very deep networks.
Name a well-known residual network architecture.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Standalone concept on an advanced architecture.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Keras for Neural Networks
current_reconciled_candidates.description: Keras is a high-level TensorFlow API that simplifies neural network construction. The Sequential model allows stacking layers; Dense layers are fully-connected; the input_shape argument specifies input dimensions; activation functions (e.g., ReLU) are set per layer.
coverage_criteria: Create a Keras Sequential model, add a Dense layer with a given number of neurons and activation, and specify input_shape.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates together cover the essential Keras API for building feedforward networks.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Overfitting and Regularization
current_reconciled_candidates.description: Overfitting occurs when a model learns training noise and fails to generalize; underfitting is the opposite. Dropout is a regularization technique that randomly drops neurons during training to prevent overfitting.
coverage_criteria: Define overfitting and underfitting with examples.
Explain how dropout works and why it reduces overfitting.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Dropout is a specific technique to combat overfitting, forming a unified concept with the general problem of overfitting.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Linear Algebra Foundations
current_reconciled_candidates.description: Neural network computations rely on linear vector spaces, inner products, norms, and linear transformations. These concepts underpin weight matrices and forward/backward passes.
coverage_criteria: Define a linear vector space and list two axioms.
Compute the dot product of two vectors and explain its role in a neuron's weighted sum.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Standalone mathematical prerequisite concept.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Gradient Descent Optimization
current_reconciled_candidates.description: Gradient descent minimizes the loss by iteratively updating parameters: w = w - η * ∇J. The learning rate η controls step size; bias is an additional parameter; Adam adapts η per parameter; an epoch is one full pass over the dataset.
coverage_criteria: Write the gradient descent update rule for a weight.
Explain the role of the learning rate and describe the advantage of the Adam optimizer.
Define epoch and distinguish it from an iteration over a single sample.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates cover the core algorithm, hyperparameters (learning rate, bias), and training loop concepts, forming a comprehensive optimization concept.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Neural Network Training Implementation
current_reconciled_candidates.description: Training involves: forward propagation to compute outputs; random weight initialization to break symmetry; a loop over epochs performing forward, cost, backward, and update steps; layer dimensions determine parameter shapes; caches store intermediate values for backprop.
coverage_criteria: List the steps in one training iteration (forward, cost, backward, update).
Explain why weights are initialized randomly and what happens if they are set to zero.
Describe the purpose of caching in forward propagation.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These low-level implementation details together form a single coherent training procedure concept.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Perceptron and Its Limitations
current_reconciled_candidates.description: The perceptron is a single neuron with step activation: output = step(∑ w_i x_i + b). Its training rule: w = w + η (d - y) x. It only solves linearly separable problems; XOR requires a hidden layer (e.g., two-layer network computing AND and OR).
coverage_criteria: Write the perceptron forward pass and training update rule.
Explain why a single perceptron cannot solve XOR and how a hidden layer enables the solution.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates explain the perceptron model, its training, the concept of linear separability, and the XOR limitation, with an explicit solution example.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Data Preparation for Neural Networks
current_reconciled_candidates.description: Non-numeric inputs must be encoded (e.g., binary encoding, one-hot encoding) for neural networks. Datasets consist of features (attributes) and a target column, and data often needs to be numeric and normalized.
coverage_criteria: Choose an encoding scheme for a categorical variable (e.g., one-hot encoding) and justify.
Given a CSV, identify the feature columns and the target column.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Both deal with preparing input data for neural networks, from encoding to dataset structure.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Divisão Treino/Teste
current_reconciled_candidates.description: A técnica de separar dados em conjuntos de treino e teste para avaliar a generalização de modelos.
coverage_criteria: O aluno deve escrever código para dividir um dataset em treino e teste.
O aluno deve explicar por que não se deve usar o mesmo conjunto para treino e teste.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Candidato único representando o conceito de divisão treino/teste.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Implementação Manual vs Bibliotecas
current_reconciled_candidates.description: Comparação entre implementar um perceptron do zero e usar scikit-learn, destacando a redução de código e complexidade.
coverage_criteria: O aluno deve listar funções do scikit-learn usadas em substituição à implementação manual.
O aluno deve identificar vantagens e desvantagens de cada abordagem.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Candidato único sobre a comparação de implementações.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Acurácia
current_reconciled_candidates.description: Métrica de avaliação que calcula a proporção de predições corretas, variando de 0 a 1.
coverage_criteria: O aluno deve calcular a acurácia a partir de predições e classes reais.
O aluno deve interpretar uma acurácia de 1.0 como separação perfeita para dados linearmente separáveis.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Candidato único sobre a métrica de acurácia.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Perceptron Multicamadas
current_reconciled_candidates.description: Introdução ao perceptron multicamadas como uma extensão para resolver problemas não-linearmente separáveis.
coverage_criteria: O aluno deve diferenciar um perceptron simples de um multicamadas pela presença de camadas ocultas.
O aluno deve justificar a necessidade de camadas múltiplas para datasets não-lineares.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Candidato único sobre perceptron multicamadas.

current_pruned_candidates.explanation: The candidate describes a specific research paper (LeCun's 1998 gradient-based learning for document recognition) which is an incidental application rather than a core teachable algorithm; the underlying backpropagation is covered by lr008.

FizzBuzz is an illustrative end-to-end application that consolidates previously taught concepts (encoding, architecture, training) without introducing a new distinct teachable idea suitable for standalone lesson coverage.

current_review_candidates.explanation: Deterministically added because cluster evaluation omitted this input candidate.
Deterministically added because cluster evaluation omitted this input candidate.

new_accepted_concepts.label: Specific lesson-local teachable idea
new_accepted_concepts.description: What the student needs to understand.
coverage_criteria: Observable check in one to three focused questions.
